title: What Happens If You Disagree With Your Architect
excerpt: Design disagreements happen on almost every project. Here's how a design-build firm handles them differently, and why having both your architect and contractor on the same team matters.
content:
You hired an architect. You trusted their vision. Then the plans came back and something feels off. Maybe the kitchen layout doesn't match what you described. Maybe the addition doesn't sit right on your Scarsdale property. Maybe the color palette or material choices just aren't what you imagined.

This happens more often than you'd think. And the way your architect responds to pushback says everything about whether you picked the right person for the job.

The Problem With Separate Teams

In most renovation and new construction projects, homeowners work with an architect, then hand those plans to a general contractor to build. The two rarely talk directly. So when you have a concern about the design, you end up in the middle of a conversation that doesn't include everyone who matters.

Your contractor might see a practical problem with what the architect drew. Your architect might not understand the site constraints until construction starts. You're stuck explaining the same thing twice, to two different people who aren't on the same page.

This setup breeds frustration. Changes cost money and time. Blame gets passed around. And your project suffers.

Why Being a Design-Build Firm Changes Everything

When your architect is also your general contractor, disagreements get resolved faster because they're discussed in one room instead of three.

Silvio M. Luca runs every project personally as both a licensed architect in Westchester, NY and a licensed general contractor. That means when a homeowner in Pelham or Mamaroneck has a concern about their kitchen remodel or second-story addition, Silvio understands both the design intent and the construction reality at the same time.

He can tell you why something was drawn a certain way. He can also tell you if it needs to change because of how your home is actually built, what your local building department requires, or what will work better in practice. He's not defending someone else's work. He's responsible for the whole thing.

That accountability matters. You're not paying for finger-pointing. You're paying for solutions.

What Actually Happens When You Disagree

A good architect listens. Not just hears you, but actually listens.

If you hired someone to handle home renovations in Westchester County and the design isn't landing for you, a real professional will ask questions. Why doesn't it feel right? What were you picturing? What's the actual problem, not just the gut feeling?

Then they explain their thinking. Not to convince you that you're wrong, but to make sure you understand the tradeoffs. Maybe the open-concept conversion you wanted in your Rye home means losing a wall that carries the second floor. Maybe the primary suite addition in your Harrison property needs to sit back further than you'd prefer because of setback requirements.

When your architect and contractor are the same person, these conversations happen before construction starts, not during it. Changes are easier to make on paper. Costs are clearer. Your input actually shapes the final result.
